item.title: REVIEW: Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 Review: Pint-Sized Power Pack
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
I’ve always hated gas generators. They’re noisy and heavy, they can be a pain in the ass to start, they fart out polluting fumes, and filling them usually involves a trip to the gas station. If I had to make a short list of great technology products that have come into their own in the last five years or so, high-capacity home backup batteries would be on it, because they free me from the tyranny of their gas-powered forebears. I’ve been trying out the $760 Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2, one of the latest in the company’s lineup of portable power packs. It’s a compact little box of energy that can crank out a steady 1,800W and features four three-prong AC outlets, two USB-C ports, one USB-A, and even a 12V lighter socket. It’s also super lightweight, at just under 24 pounds, and even has a nice swinging handle to help you carry it around. A compact, powerful-enough backup battery with plenty of ports. The 1000 Plus v2 is not totally perfect. It’s got a noisy, eager cooling fan, it takes a little doing to get it to recharge to full power, and it doesn’t have the full UL certification I’d like to see. But if you don’t need the larger batteries out there, it’s an ideal companion for camping trips, small power-tool use, and one-day outings where you need highly portable power. There’s no real setup for the HomePower 1000 Plus out of the box—you can start using it right away when you unpack it. (The unit I received arrived with a 28% battery charge.) You should still connect it to Jackery’s app, which just involves scanning for the device over Bluetooth, tapping its icon when it appears, then going through a brief setup that involves adding it to your Wi-Fi network, if you’d like. Once added to the app, the 1000 Plus v2’s home screen shows the battery’s current percentage and operating temperature, which ports are in use, and how many watts they’re outputting. This screen also contains basic controls like toggling ports on and off, activating the bright LED light on the device’s front, and flipping on the battery’s display. If your electric company offers a time-of-use (ToU) plan, you can use the 1000 Plus v2 to save a little money by diving into the app’s settings and configuring it to deliver power during peak hours (when energy costs more) and recharge when electricity is cheaper. When getting that ready, you can also enter your per-kWh prices for peak and off-peak hours. Back on the battery’s home page, you’ll then see an estimate of how much ToU mode has saved you. Another setting purportedly lets you limit the charging speed to anywhere between 100W and 1,800W. That’s a little confusing, since the device is actually limited to 1,600W recharging, according to its official specs. It also only climbed to (and stayed at) 1,060W when I first tested it; I had to turn on “Emergency Charging” in the app’s settings to reach 1,600W. I asked Jackery if the 1,800W option is a mistake or if there’s actually a way to reach that, and will update this story if it responds. Elsewhere in the settings, you can set some outlets to “priority” and others to “non-priority,” which tells the battery to shut off the latter when it reaches a level you set. That can be nice if you want to shut off other devices but keep a key appliance running as the battery wanes. The AC ports on other backup batteries I’ve tested—the DJI Power 2000 and the Anker Solix S2000—lack this kind of control and are either all on or all off. Most of the remaining settings focus on battery-saving measures, such as turning off Wi-Fi, turning off the battery if nothing has drawn power from it for a set period, and so on. These options are more or less the same ones that you’ll find on the Solix S2000, although the Jackery lacks any sort of analog to that device’s “Storm Guard” feature, which allows the battery to automatically recharge itself if the National Weather Service issues a storm warning for your area. That’s not a problem if you’re using the 1000 Plus v2 only as needed, but you could be left in a lurch if the power goes out after it’s been discharging all day during peak hours in ToU mode. Jackery packed a lot into this little guy, although things can get crowded—the four AC outlets are necessarily very close together, which could be an issue if you’re using large wall-wart-style plugs. Other than that, it’s all gravy: one of its USB-C ports outputs 140W, which is higher than the 100W you see on most 1kWh batteries. (The other is 30W.) And there’s a bright, circular LED that’s about the size of a quarter. It would be helpful when camping, although I could see the broad light strip on the front of the similar Anker Solix C1000 being even nicer. When using the HomePower 1000 Plus V2 around my apartment, I really appreciated its 24-pound weight, compact size, and swinging handle. It was easy to schlep from one room to the next, and its 12-inch-by-9-inch footprint is very forgiving in terms of placement. I started testing by checking how long the 1000 Plus v2 could last with its AC ports, display, and wireless connections active but nothing else drawing power. It lost 14% of its battery while running only the AC inverter for 24 hours. Just doing some back-of-the-envelope math, that’s an ambient loss of about 246Wh, or roughly 10W per hour, which is on the low end for 1kWh batteries like this. I also redid the refrigerator test I ran with the Solix S2000, which involved, well, plugging my fridge into the battery and seeing how long it could last with normal use. I found that I missed the S2000’s rear AC outlets, which let me hide the fridge’s cable in the back. Once I plugged the thing into the front, it ran for about 22.5 hours before the Jackery’s battery dropped to 3% and I switched the appliance back to the wall. That’s a little past the 19 hours quoted in a chart on the 1000 Plus’s product page, although my result is probably a best-case scenario because I don’t open my fridge more than three or four times in a day. The Solix S2000, which has twice the capacity, could power it about twice as long. Jackery’s specs mostly held up when I challenged them. Its AC ports handled higher wattages just fine; at a peak of over 1,700W, it seemed to keep going as long as it had the charge to run. If I exceeded 1,800W, as I did when I threw a hair dryer and a small space heater at it that pushed a combined 2,070W (well shy of the Jackery’s 3,600W peak surge capacity), the device ran both for about a minute until its AC output cut off and the Jackery app sent an AC output failure push notification on my phone. That was what I’d expected would happen, but all the same, it’s good to know you shouldn’t expect this battery to run a hair dryer and space heater simultaneously. It also shows that the 1000 Plus can clearly handle the initial surge required to start the motors of many smaller electric power tools. The 140W and 30W USB-C ports worked as expected, too. The battery hit 170W while powering an Anker Prime 300W power bank, which can simultaneously charge itself via its own dual USB-C ports. I particularly like that Jackery includes a 12V cigarette lighter DC port on this and other batteries, which handled the 100W my lightweight AstroAI portable air compressor requires just fine. It has always felt silly to turn on a whole car just to use this thing, and midwestern winters have made me wary of ever using my car’s battery for anything other than starting the engine. Using a compact battery is much more convenient. I wasn’t able to test the two DC8020 inputs on the battery’s side, which can accept up to 400W of solar charging from as many as four solar panels if you have a splitter that Jackery sells. It’s inconvenient that the company went with the DC8020 over other, more common ports used by most portable solar panels. As one reviewer at GearJunkie noted, that means you’re likely to need an adapter for third-party equipment, which just adds a point of failure. Jackery says it uses the DC8020 to bridge various connector standards, such as MC4 and XT60. I don’t have enough experience with solar power to have a strong opinion about this, except to say that my life has been better since most small tech moved to USB-C, and these various solar connector standards remind me of the bad times before that. Something I didn’t like about the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 was its fan noise. A degree of loud whirring is inevitable when you’re using a station, but Jackery’s is definitely louder than the only slightly larger Solix S2000. When I used it to power my TV and other devices in UPS mode, its fan periodically spun up loudly enough that I needed to turn the volume up a few clicks. That only happened when the battery was charging and discharging at the same time, though—in ToU mode or with the battery unplugged from the wall, it stayed quiet. On the plus side, the 1000 Plus v2 otherwise makes for a solid uninterruptible power supply, or UPS. Jackery says the machine can switch your devices from wall power to battery within 10 milliseconds. When I tested that claim by unplugging the 1000 Plus while playing games on my TV, I couldn’t tell the difference. If the 1000 Plus v2 unexpectedly loses wall power, you’ll get a push notification from the Jackery app, so you can find out about an outage even if you’re watching TV in complete darkness. Another plus is that the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 is expandable to 11kWh with Jackery’s $1,000 Battery Pack 2000 Plus v2, a stackable battery pack that adds an extra 2kWh of capacity. That’s quite a bit higher than similar portable 1kWh power stations like the EcoFlow Delta 3 Portable Power Station, which can only be expanded to 5kWh, or the Solix C1000, which has a max expansion of 2,112Wh. The Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 is a great compact power station. Its 1,024Wh capacity makes it a solid option for backing up low-power appliances during power outages, and its 1,800W output is sufficient for many around-the-house, short-term use cases. Plus, its lightweight, roughly foot-wide body is a boon for placement around the house or packing for camping trips. My complaints about this device are few and mostly concern the absence of nice-to-haves. I wish it would charge itself if a storm is imminent, for instance, if I’m using it to save money on a ToU plan. The fan noise is also a bit much compared to that of other, larger 2kWh power stations I’ve tested, but it’s not disqualifyingly loud by any means. One reason not to buy the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 is its $760 price tag. While it does beat competitors on expandability, the EcoFlow Delta 3 and Anker Solix C1000 can both be had for $700 and $600, respectively, and each features six AC outlets rather than four (although three of the EcoFlow’s are two-prong). They may both be easier to justify, depending on what you’re after. But if being able to add more batteries later is a big deal to you, it’s hard to beat the compact, lightweight HomePower 1000 Plus v2.

item.title: REVIEW: Seagate One Touch 4TB external hard drive review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
As a standard portable 4TB HDD, this mechanical drive performs surprisingly well for backup and archieve, and if you want to use it as a working drive for lightweight video work, that’s perfectly possible. However, its real strength is the software Toolkit, which enables fast backups of all your computer files, plus strong password protection, all at a relatively reasonable price. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The Seagate One Touch 4TB is a relatively nondescript-looking portable HDD which is bus-powered directly through the USB-C data cable. The drive is relatively compact and slips easily into a laptop bag or pocket, making it highly portable. Whilst the exterior casing is mid-grey plastic, it’s nicely finished and feels robust. This portable drive features an HDD rather than an SSD, which does make this drive cheaper than some of the latest ultrafast drives I’ve looked at recently. Even so, at £179/US$199 at the time of writing this review, it’s still relatively expensive. For that money, you get the drive itself and a short 50cm USB-C cable to connect it to your machine. Getting started is easy: the drive comes formatted in exFAT, so it’s easily recognised on Mac, PC, and Linux systems. Opening on either iOS or Windows machines reveals free software that guides you through initial registration, downloads the Security Toolkit, and highlights partner deals Seagate has set up with Adobe, Synology, and Mylio. In this review, I’ve downloaded and installed the Toolkit, which is basically split into two parts. It includes a backup feature, which lets you choose different backup options for your computer and drive, and a security option, which lets you add a password and encrypt the drive’s contents. Alongside those software options, there are also partner deals, and all offer a limited trial period before you have to move to a full subscription. However, the Synology Deep Search is well worth mentioning. Whilst you only get six months of free use before needing to pay, if you need to manage multiple files and have a search feature driven by AI that is far better than your standard search options, especially on a Mac, then this really might be of interest. As a standard portable HDD, the 4TB capacity is perfect if you work with media files and need space for HD and 4K video. Whilst HDD technology limits speed, the benchmarking tests still showed impressive transfer rates, reaching over 140MB/s in some tests for both read and write. That transfer speed let me edit 4K footage shot on the GoPro Mission 1 ILS directly from the drive in Final Cut Pro X, and while the machine and drive occasionally had to catch up, editing a five-minute production was extremely smooth. Its real strength, however, is securely backing up your laptop or desktop data, and the included Toolkit software lets you run through a series of setup options with easy-to-follow prompts that work on both Mac and PC. Unlike many HDD and SSD portable drives that offer software encryption, this drive offers hardware AES 256-bit encryption that is managed through the Seagate Toolkit software. For my money, that makes it one of the best external hard drives for security. Through that software, you can encrypt the drive with a password lock. Because this security is hardware-based rather than software, it also meant that, through the benchmarking, when I tested the drive before and after the hardware encryption had been activated, the performance difference was minimal. It’s obvious from the aesthetics and material choices that this is a mid-range portable HDD, but the tests impressed me with its performance and overall quality. I'd definitely recommend it if you’re looking for a middle-of-the-road, no-frills, high-capacity HDD for general storage and backup, with the real value here being the Toolkit included with the drive. Seagate One Touch 4TB: Price and availability - Where can you get it? Directly from Seagate and online retailers. At present, the Seagate One Touch portable HDD is available in two different capacities - 2TB and 4TB, which retail for $160 and $200 respectively. In the UK, it's priced at £112 and £176. You can buy it direct from the Seagate website, where you'll also find a list of all stockists, which includes most major main online retailers. It comes in three colors: blue, grey, and white. Power: USB-powered, no external adapter required Security: Password protection and hardware encryption Lifting the drive from the box, and the 4TB version I’m looking at feels nice and tactile, with a wave surface texture that adds a little interest to the mid-grey colouring. The full build is plastic, yet it feels decent enough, with a single USB-C port at the back and, thankfully, a small white indicator LED right next to it. In terms of size and weight, it’s just a little larger than the compact 2.5-inch laptop-style HDD inside, with the casing measuring 115.3 × 80 × 20.9mm. The 4TB version I’ve looked at in this review weighs 268g. The USB-C cable is a bit longer than the ones I’ve seen with some other portable drives recently, measuring 50cm, which gives good reach to a desktop mini PC or laptop, depending on what you’re using. Whilst the One Touch name initially suggests fingerprint security, it actually refers to the company’s product line that offers one-click backup for your files. It also offers automatic backup folder mirroring and is plug-and-play, so the name really reflects how simple the drive is to use. Alongside the hardware comes a software suite, with installers on the drive's root that you can run once you plug it in. The drive comes pre-formatted in exFAT, but you can reformat it to match your native OS, Mac or PC. The software installer lets you install the files you need for the more advanced backup and security features, and I liked how streamlined the installation process was, with it guiding you through the initial setup step by step. The Seagate One Touch portable external hard drive is sold by the company as a premium portable, on-the-go backup solution, designed to be used equally in the home or out and about. This high-capacity portable hard drive comes with software options ready to install. These let you back up and secure your files, while software partnerships offer extended trial periods for apps to help you manage and organise files on the drive and on your host machine. The drive is available in three colour options: dark blue, space grey, and white. It’s also provided with a long USB-C cable, at 50cm, that runs from the drive to your host machine. This means your machine needs a USB-C port to work with this drive. The drive comes with bundled software, including the Seagate Toolkit, which requires registration but no other subscription costs. There’s also a two-month trial of Adobe Creative Cloud Pro, and six-month trials of Mylio and Synology Deep Search. You also get the superb Seagate Rescue Data Recovery Service. If the worst happens to your files, you can send the drive to Seagate, and they will see if they can recover anything that still exists. While this drive can be used as a portable working drive, Seagate has marketed this as a portable backup solution, and as such, it doesn’t highlight the transfer rate. However, with USB 3.2 Gen 1, essentially USB 3, you can expect a maximum theoretical bandwidth of 5Gbps, 625MB/s. However, since this contains an HDD, we can expect transfer rates between 120 and 150MB/s, which suggests Seagate matched the internal hardware and USB interface to maximise performance for its intended use as a portable backup rather than a working drive. CrystalDiskMark: Read 147.15MB/s; Write 146.06MB/s AJA System Test Lite: Read 132MB/s; Write 127MB/s ATTO Disk Benchmark: Read 133.55MB/s; Write 133.45MB/s AS SSD: Read 137.86MB/s; Write 130.28MB/s Getting started with the Seagate One Touch 4TB portable HDD is as easy as with any portable drive, and in this test, I used it on the MacBook Pro M1 Max and the HP EliteBook XG 21 laptop, along with a series of mini PCs. As I moved from macOS to Windows 11 Pro and Home, the Seagate One Touch performed similarly across all operating systems, which is great to see, and the simple USB-C connection was fully compatible with all the operating systems I tried. Because the drive came pre-formatted in exFAT, it was instantly recognised on both Mac and PC. I first installed the software on the MacBook Pro M1 Max to check out the backup options and security features, and I was impressed by how easy it was to set up. The initial stage requires you to register the drive and create a Seagate account, but once that’s done, it guides you through downloading the Seagate Toolkit installer, installing it, and then walking you through the setup options one after the other. For backup on the Mac, even though I have Time Machine activated, I selected a portion of my MacBook Pro’s hard drive, and once that initial setup was complete, the backup process started. What I like about the Toolkit is that it’s quick to access, and you can edit your backup plan at any time. Another point is that if you need to use the machine during a backup, as I did when I initially set up the plan, you can pause it so it doesn’t slow down your system, then restart it later. You can then schedule it to run overnight when you’re not using the machine. Likewise, on the PC, which doesn’t have such a sophisticated backup system as part of the OS, you can choose to mirror your mini PC, desktop, or laptop hard drive, and the registration and initiation process is just as easy. The second part of the included software is the security option, which uses AES 256-bit encryption and is activated through the Security Toolkit on both Mac and PC. It takes a little more setup, you need to enable certain security options and unplug and re-plug the drive for the installation to complete. But again, it’s extremely well documented, and the software guides you through every step, including adding an email address and phone number in case you forget the password you set. As backup software and an off-the-shelf, easy-to-use solution, this is as good as any paid option out there and is certainly easy to get your head around. Those two bits of bundled software really do balance the added cost of a standard 4TB portable HDD, and if you are looking for something cheaper, Seagate does make cheaper portable HDDs with this capacity. If you’re using this for business or your home office, I would highly recommend paying the extra for those security and backup features, since you’re only paying an extra $40 / £40 compared with the non-secure options. When it comes to performance, I used the drive for quick video editing in Final Cut Pro X and then CapCut, using files from the GoPro Mission 1 ILS. I was impressed by how fast this drive’s transfer rates were, both reading the files from the drive and writing the final render back to it during the test. I started with a simple HD edit, and even with footage shot in GoPro Log, it supplied and wrote data at the speed the system demanded. Even when I upgraded to 4K footage, it was still more than capable, with only the occasional pause as files were written. I’d still opt for an SSD over an HDD, but if you are caught out and need large-capacity storage on the move, then this will do the job. The only issue is that it doesn’t dissipate heat well, so it will thermal throttle during longer editing sessions. However, when I switched to editing stills shot on the Sony A7 IV and scans of Ilford FP4 Plus, the drive was more than capable of handling edits in DxO PhotoLab on the Mac and PC. As this drive is designed for archiving, it's a great option for small businesses looking for machine backup, photographers who want a solid, portable drive they can use in and out of the studio or anyone wanting a portable backup drive. The plastic exterior is lightweight, and it feels relatively robust. Plus, you can password-protect it for security. The Seagate One Touch 4TB portable HDD is a great all-round option for backup and a decent secure working drive for light media use. The design and build lean a bit toward plastic, but because it uses a single cable for power and data, you don’t have to carry a separate power supply, which makes it extremely convenient for field use. It’s clear this is designed as a backup drive rather than a working drive, and with HDD rather than SSD technology, transfer rates are slower. So if you are looking for a high-capacity working drive, this is perfectly capable, but you might want to look at an SSD option. This drive is marketed and better suited to backup and archive use, and the 4TB of capacity at this price is well balanced. What really sets this drive apart, and gives it an edge over many others, is its AES 256-bit hardware encryption, plus software that's exceptionally straightforward and easy to use. There’s just nothing complex about it. It does the job without going into any major complexities and offers excellent fallback when you need it. Whilst the aesthetics and build quality are very middle of the road, it’s all solid enough. After carrying the drive around for a week in my kit bag, it stood up to knocks and bashes without much issue, proving the plastic exterior is as robust as many metal options. If you are in the market for a high-capacity portable backup drive with hardware encryption and excellent bundled software, then I would highly recommend the Seagate One Touch 4TB HDD. It’s a well-balanced storage option without any aesthetic frills, with a main focus on pure functionality. Should I buy the Seagate One Touch 4TB? Buy it if... You need portable, high-capacity storage. This drive is built for high-capacity storage, with large internal drive options and a fast USB Type-C connection to your host machine. You want easy backup and security. The bundled software is about as good as I’ve seen for this type of portable HDD, offering easy backup and security in just a few clicks, with no complexity. Don't buy it if... You need high performance. While the HDD's performance is exceptionally good, its transfer rates are far slower than you’d expect from a standard SSD. You need physical and data security. While AES 256-bit hardware security gives you peace of mind that people won’t be able to access your files if you lose the drive, the physical design, while it will stand a knock or two, isn’t built as a tough, go-anywhere drive. item.title: REVIEW: CRKD Nitro Deck 2 review: a great but heavy Switch 2 handheld controller
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The CRKD Nitro Deck 2 is an all-encompassing handheld solution for the Switch and Switch 2, offering a multiplatform controller, backplate protection, and a kickstand all in one unit. There are some ergonomic and minor connectivity issues, but the Nitro Deck 2 is hard to beat if you want the ultimate handheld experience on Nintendo’s platforms. - -Slightly awkward back button placements Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The CRKD Nitro Deck 2 is primarily billed as a Nintendo Switch 2 controller for handheld use, but it offers a lot more besides. It's CRKD’s follow-up to the Nitro Deck and Nitro Deck+, two previous accessories aimed at the original Nintendo Switch. The CRKD Nitro Deck 2 has a functional design focused more on ergonomics than style, although some of the colorways add some panache; the Pal Grey variant I reviewed, for instance, harked back to retro Nintendo controllers, thanks to its colorful face buttons and darker grey accents. The Nitro Deck 2 fits to the Switch and Switch 2 by clamping on the sides of the unit, rather than actually connecting to the Joy-Con 2 slots. A small button on the back clicks and twists to tightly grip your console, and tight it is; even when I held it upside down, my console didn’t move an inch. You can then connect to your console wirelessly via Bluetooth or wired by using the included U-shaped USB adapter. CRKD’s mobile app can be used to remap the inputs of the Nitro Deck 2, as well as enable the ‘No Deadzone’ mode for the joysticks. Its interface is clear and easy to use, and I didn’t experience any bugs. One downside, though, is that you have to reconnect to the app every time you open it by holding two buttons for three seconds, which limits the convenience of back-and-forth adjustments. All the buttons feel great, providing plenty of clicky feedback and responsiveness. The back buttons are awkwardly placed, though, and I found myself accidentally triggering them on occasion. The real highlight of the Nitro Deck 2, though, is its joysticks. Not only are they precise and responsive, but they also feature dials that let you adjust their tension at any point, which is an excellent design choice and should allow any gamer to get their preferred feel. Unfortunately, poor ergonomics detract from the Nitro Deck 2’s otherwise positive performance aspects. Not only do the pads angle inwards at the bottom, contrary to the majority of gamepads, but it’s also heavy when loaded with a console. These factors can make it cumbersome and awkward to use, especially when trying to game upright. The Nitro Deck 2 is easy to pair to the Switch or Switch 2 via Bluetooth, although it takes a while to reconnect to your console after sleeping. Reconnection is quicker in wired mode, but it’s still not instantaneous. It was also easy to pair with PC and Android devices, although it’s a shame you can’t switch between them without having to pair each time. The battery life of the Nitro Deck 2 is reasonable, lasting for as long as CRKD claims (15-20 hours), according to my testing. It’s a small inconvenience that you have to charge it separately from your console, though. When you consider all that it offers, the Nitro Deck 2 represents good value. Not only are you getting handheld pads for the Switch 1 and Switch 2, but you’re also getting protection for your console, a standalone controller you can use with other platforms besides Nintendo’s, and a kickstand. Comfort issues do hamper the experience somewhat, but if you don’t mind holding a weighty unit, the Nitro Deck 2 is a fine choice as a versatile gamepad. CRKD Nitro Deck 2 review: Price & availability - Good price for a versatile handheld gamepad The Nitro Deck 2 costs $89.99 / £89.99 / AU$161 and is available now in four colorways: Smoke Black, Pal Grey, LRG Fusion, and White. It comes with a USB cable, a double-ended USB adapter, and a legacy adapter for Switch 1 compatibility. The joystick caps and D-pad hat are replaceable, but no extra sets for either are included in the box. This is a reasonable price for a unit that’s not only a Switch and Switch 2 handheld case and handheld controller, but also a standalone gamepad for PC and mobile, both wired and wireless. You won’t find many more complete solutions for your Switch 2 than this, or even third-party substitutes for the Joy-Con 2 controllers, save for a few examples, such as the Mobapad M12 HD and M12S. A more left-field alternative to the Nitro Deck 2 is the GameSir G8+, a Bluetooth mobile controller that doesn’t officially support the Switch 2, but users have reported compatibility with the system. If you just want a more comfortable handheld experience for your Switch 2 while sticking with the Joy-Con 2 pads, the Genki Attack Vector is a reasonably priced solution that offers three sets of grips as well as a backplate cover. What’s more, it can remain attached to your console when docked. CRKD Nitro Deck 2 review: Design & features The Nitro Deck 2 has an appearance that’s more about function than form, with its soft edges and curves being more about ergonomics than aesthetics. It’s a fetching piece of design nonetheless, and the Pal Grey finish of my review unit added a retro appeal, with its dark grey accents and colorful face buttons alluding to the classic SNES controller. The build quality is respectable, too. Although the plastic shell didn’t initially strike me as being particularly premium, I quickly felt its solidity and sturdiness once I held it in my hands. The sliding mechanisms for both pads operate smoothly as well. Rather than the pads of the Nitro Deck 2 actually attaching to each Joy-Con slot on the Switch or Switch 2, they simply clamp to the sides of the console without actually inserting into these slots. To tighten the clamp, you simply push and twist the button on the rear of the unit. This requires a fair amount of force, and so does releasing it to remove the console, but I wouldn’t say it was overly arduous, and it’s worth the effort for the secure fit it provides. When attached, the Switch 2 fits snugly and securely; I had no worries about it coming loose, as there wasn’t a hint of looseness. The unit also aligns precisely with the dimensions and contours of the Switch 2, although my one small gripe is that accessing the game card flap can be fiddly, as there’s little room to reach down to lift it up. This isn’t an issue when the Nitro Deck 2 is attached to the Switch 1, though, since the flap on that console opens the other way. Speaking of which, the Nitro Deck 2 fits just as well to the Switch 1 as it does to the Switch 2. Thanks to the included legacy adapter, its USB-C port is still accessible, so you can still have a wired connection between the console and the Nitro Deck 2. This wired connection to both the Switch 1 and 2 is handled by another adapter, a double-ended U-shaped USB-C jack, that slots into the bottom of the Deck and the console. The Nitro Deck 2 also features a kickstand on the back, allowing you to use your console with another controller. This is made of metal and feels very solid. It’s also very sturdy when open, and it folds flush into the back of the Deck. It can be a little difficult to release it from its clip, but this is a small price to pay for its secure fastening. To customize the inputs of the extra shoulder and back buttons, you can use the M button in combination with others to alter the mapping. However, you can also use CRKD’s mobile app, where you can remap every button, as well as enable a ‘No Deadzone’ mode for the joysticks in order to increase their sensitivity. The app is clearly laid out and easy to navigate, and I didn’t experience any bugs or glitches, which was somewhat of a surprise given the poor rating it has on app stores. For some bizarre reason, though, it only operates in landscape mode, but more frustrating is the fact that switching between the app and your console isn’t exactly a seamless experience; you have to hold the Home button and the left D-pad button for 3 seconds every time you go back to the app after exiting it. While its grips may look ergonomic, I struggled to get entirely comfortable with the Nitro Deck 2. Partly, this is due to the sheer weight of the unit when loaded with a console, which makes holding it upright a chore, even for short periods. But the other half of the problem stems from the grips’ orientation. They protrude outwards at the top rather than at the bottom, running counter to the best Nintendo Switch 2 controller shapes, and are at a less natural angle for your hands. I did acclimatize to their form somewhat, but I was never entirely at ease with it. I also found the back buttons awkward to use, as they were too low down to align with my natural finger placement around the grips. Their low travel and resistance meant there were times when I accidentally triggered them, too. These issues aside, though, the Nitro Deck 2 offers fantastic performance. The face buttons are clicky and satisfying to use, while the D-pad is very comfortable thanks to its circular hat. Its floating design also meant presses had plenty of travel, which in turn created good feedback. I found the shoulder buttons were easy to reach and use as well. The best input of all, though, is the joysticks, which feature dials at their bases for adjusting resistance on the fly. This is a great idea and one I wish more controllers implemented. Looser settings allow for easy maneuvering and quick flicks, while tighter settings give you more control and precision. The Nitro Deck 2 also features motion controls. I found these to be accurate and responsive when aiming with the bow in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, although using them in handheld mode isn’t exactly practical, given the whole console moves with your hands. Unfortunately, I did experience some small connectivity issues with the Nitro Deck 2. Although pairing with my consoles was a relatively quick process, it can be slow to reconnect when you wake your console. It activated quicker when I used a wired connection, but it wasn’t instant. The Nitro Deck 2 worked just as well with my Switch 1 as it did with my Switch 2. It’s a shame, though, that the aforementioned legacy adapter doesn’t support console charging. I’m not sure whether this was a particular issue with my review unit or a known limitation, but either way it’s a shame from a convenience perspective. As for other platforms, I had no issues connecting or using the Nitro Deck 2 with PC or my Android smartphone via Bluetooth, although hot-switching isn’t possible, with pairing required each time you move between devices. The battery life of the Nitro Deck 2 is reasonable — according to my testing, it lasts about as long as CRKD claims it can, which is between 15 and 20 hours. However, it’s a shame you can’t charge your console and the Deck with a single cable, as there’s no passthrough feature. Should I buy the CRKD Nitro Deck 2? With the instantly adjustable tension for the joysticks, every gamer should be able to get the right feel. Not only does the Nitro Deck 2 work with the Switch and Switch 2 in handheld mode, but it can also be used to game on PC and mobile devices. You want something light and very portable With a console attached, the Nitro Deck 2 is noticeably heavy and bulky in the hand. The Nitro Deck 2 doesn’t wake up instantly with your console, and switching between devices requires repairing. Although not explicitly marketed as a Switch 2 controller, user reports suggest that the G8+ does indeed work with the console. When we tested it on mobile devices, we were impressed with its comfortable grips and smooth, precise thumbsticks and triggers. Read our full GameSir G8+ review. If you want to stick with the Joy-Con 2 pads but require better handheld ergonomics, Genki’s accessory may just fit the bill. It comes with three sets of grips to accommodate all kinds of hands, while the back cover adds some protection to your Switch 2 without compromising its fit in the dock (unlike the Nitro Deck 2). Read our full Genki Attack Vector review. I tested the Nitro Deck 2 for over a week, using it with both the Switch and Switch 2, as well as with a PC and my Android smartphone. I tested both wired and wireless connections. I also tested CRKD’s companion mobile app. I played games such as Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, both of which are good tests for the responsiveness of the buttons and comfort of the D-pad. I also played The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which is a great test of all facets of a controller, including the motion controls. I’ve been gaming for decades and have plenty of experience testing controllers and other peripherals for numerous platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2. I’ve also reviewed other Switch 2 accessories, including handheld grips.

item.title: REVIEW: Vivo X500 Pro Max first impressions: Vivo came to play, and the competition should be nervous
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
Vivo could have played it safe with the X500 series. Give the phones a slightly faster processor, slap on a new coat of paint, throw around a few AI buzzwords, and call it a day. Nobody would have been particularly surprised. Thankfully, Vivo seems to have had other ideas. The new X500 lineup consists of three phones: the X500, X500 Pro, and X500 Pro Max. But don’t let the names fool you into thinking these are simply three sizes of the same phone. Each model has its own identity, with differences in display size, processing power, and camera hardware. The X500 gets a 6.59-inch display and the Dimensity 9600M, while the compact X500 Pro packs a 6.36-inch screen and the flagship Dimensity 9600 Pro. Then there’s the X500 Pro Max, the big boss of the family, with a larger display, upgraded cameras, and the same flagship silicon. I’ve got the Vivo X500 Pro Max in my hands, and there’s already plenty to get excited about. One important caveat, though: this is the global version, not the Chinese variant. The global launch is coming soon, so we’ll have to wait a little longer to see what the entire family brings to the table. For now, let’s talk about the phone that has caught my attention. Design and build: Subtle flex, maximum effect I’ve got the gray version, and honestly, this is the one I’d pick. The rear panel doesn’t scream for attention, but look a little closer, and there’s more going on than meets the eye. The lower half of the back has a matte finish sprinkled with tiny star-like details that shimmer when the light hits them. The upper half gets a slightly raised section with a different texture, although the entire surface remains smooth to the touch. It’s understated, classy, and just flashy enough to remind you that this isn’t some run-of-the-mill slab of glass. The camera island is still massive, because apparently smartphone manufacturers have collectively decided that subtle camera bumps are a thing of the past. At least Vivo has dressed it up with a color-matched ring, while the flash has switched from a line-shaped design to a circular one. Elsewhere, it’s business as usual, and that’s not a complaint. You get flat glass on the back, flat aluminum rails, and a flat display. The phone also retains its IP69 dust and water resistance rating, so a little rain shouldn’t send you into panic mode. The box includes a case, a USB cable, and a 90W charging adapter. Vivo also continues to offer an optional Photographer Kit with a shoulder strap, an extra quick-release hook, and a case featuring a camera control grip. There’s one accessory I wish the global version had borrowed from its Chinese sibling: a second case designed around the newer rear display, which lets you control the rear cameras when taking selfies. Because if you’re going to take selfies, why not use the better cameras? Sadly, global buyers miss out on this particular party trick. The X500 Pro Max gets a 6.85-inch AMOLED display, up from 6.78 inches on last year’s model. That’s bigger than the screen on the X300 Ultra, too. The resolution also matches the Ultra, giving the Pro Max a welcome bump over its predecessor. Peak brightness remains at an impressive 4,500 nits, while LTPO technology allows the refresh rate to adapt to what’s happening on the screen. This time, it can climb all the way to 144Hz. Translation: scrolling should feel ridiculously smooth, and animations should look slick. You also get an always-on display that can stay enabled permanently, an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor, USB 3.2 connectivity, dual stereo speakers, and four microphones. There’s still no dedicated camera button, but I can’t say I’m losing sleep over it. The customizable shortcut key is sticking around, and I’d much rather have a button I can configure to do what I want than another piece of hardware I might barely use. Performance: Two nanometers of trouble for the competition Here’s where things get properly interesting. The X500 Pro Max is the first phone to run MediaTek’s new 2nm Dimensity 9600 Pro chipset. Yes, two nanometers. We’re now at the point where smartphone processors sound like they belong in a physics lecture. The chip uses ARM’s latest CPU and GPU designs, with two ultra-prime cores clocked at 4.55GHz, three performance cores at 4.35GHz, and three additional cores at 3.1GHz. MediaTek also claims a 27% improvement in peak GPU performance. That’s a promising combination of raw power and improved efficiency, particularly for demanding games, intensive multitasking, and AI workloads. The chipset also supports LPDDR6 RAM and UFS 5 storage, although Vivo hasn’t confirmed whether the tested phone uses those newer standards or sticks with LPDDR5X memory and UFS 4.1 storage. We will talk more in depth in our full review. On the software front, OriginOS 7 runs on Android 17. OriginOS 6 was a significant step forward, so the latest version feels more like a refinement than a complete overhaul. The interface remains slick, and Vivo has added AI features, fluid motion, seamless interaction, and a new Snap Up Engine for system optimization. I’m not complaining about the familiar look. If something works this well, there’s no need to tear it apart just to make the update feel important. I’ll save the final verdict on performance for the full review. Cameras: The Ultra’s zoom, minus some of its bragging rights Vivo has refreshed almost the entire camera system, and the periscope telephoto camera is the star of the show. It’s the same unit found in the X300 Ultra, which is excellent news for anyone who enjoys zooming in without turning their photos into impressionist paintings. Honestly, the Vivo X500 Pro Max isn’t just chasing megapixels. It’s bringing some serious camera technology to the party, starting with one of Sony’s latest 50MP, 1/1.28-inch LOFIC CMOS image sensors. And no, LOFIC isn’t just another acronym for a marketing department to get excited about. Short for Lateral Overflow Integration Capacitor, LOFIC technology promises high dynamic range (HDR) images with less processing overhead. Instead of capturing multiple frames and stitching them together to preserve highlights, shadows, and details while controlling noise, the sensor can achieve similar results with a single shot. For content creators, that’s a pretty big deal. Moving subjects are less likely to end up looking like accidental double exposures, thanks to a reduced risk of ghosting. The technology also enables more efficient HDR 4K video recording at 60 frames per second while lowering power consumption. Your footage gets the upgrade, without your battery necessarily paying the price. The camera hardware doesn’t stop there. The X500 Pro Max retains a 200MP telephoto camera and a 50MP ultrawide shooter, complementing the new main sensor. Features such as 4K Cinematic Colour Video, Auto-framing, and Stage Mode 3.0 further position this phone as a serious tool for creators rather than just another expensive rectangle for social media scrolling. Want to get closer to distant subjects? Vivo also offers optional 200mm and 400mm telephoto extender lenses, much like those available for the X300 Ultra. These accessories open up additional possibilities for long-range photography and creative framing. Just remember that they’re sold separately, because apparently getting closer to your subject comes with an additional price tag. But no, the X500 Pro Max doesn’t steal every advantage from its Ultra sibling. But with upgrades to every camera except the selfie shooter, Vivo clearly hasn’t treated photography as an afterthought. Thankfully, the cameras appear to be where Vivo wants to make the biggest noise. First impressions: This is how you do an annual upgrade The biggest surprise about the Vivo X500 Pro Max is just how much Vivo has changed. A larger display, a new 2nm flagship chipset, refreshed cameras, and a massive battery are not the sort of upgrades I’d dismiss as incremental. The Chinese version gets an 8,000mAh battery, while the global model, which is our unit, comes in at 7,800mAh. That’s a serious amount of battery for a flagship, especially when paired with a chip designed to improve efficiency. Wired charging remains at 90W, with 40W wireless charging for those who prefer to ditch the cable. Of course, impressive specifications don’t automatically make a great phone. I still need to test battery endurance, sustained performance, camera consistency, and how well the software holds up during everyday use. I went into the Vivo X500 Pro Max expecting a decent flagship refresh. Instead, Vivo seems determined to make the competition work a little harder. A massive 7,800mAh battery, a 2nm flagship chipset, a sharper 144Hz display, and meaningful camera upgrades make this feel like more than a yearly exercise in changing numbers on a spec sheet. The camera system is particularly intriguing. With a new Sony 50MP LOFIC main sensor designed to capture HDR images in a single shot, a 200MP periscope telephoto camera, and a 50MP ultrawide shooter, Vivo appears to be taking mobile photography seriously. The promise of reduced subject ghosting and more efficient HDR 4K video recording at 60fps could make this an especially compelling option for content creators. Add support for optional telephoto extender lenses, and the X500 Pro Max starts looking like a rather capable camera that happens to make phone calls. Of course, the real test is still ahead. Battery endurance, sustained performance, and camera consistency will determine whether the X500 Pro Max is genuinely great or simply looks impressive on paper. But Vivo has already given me plenty of reasons to be optimistic. The X500 Pro Max doesn’t look like a phone that exists merely to justify a new number on the box. It looks like Vivo actually sat down, identified what mattered, and decided to do something about it. If the full review backs up these early impressions, Vivo might have a serious flagship contender on its hands. And if other smartphone makers are watching, here’s a friendly suggestion: take notes. Also, in the meantime, here’s our Vivo X300 Ultra review.

item.title: REVIEW: Lavazza MilkEasy Plus review: affordable frothing made easy
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus is an excellent-value milk frother that delivers superb performance without the hefty price tag. Delivering a versatile range of modes, great performance across both dairy and plant-based milks, and simple controls, it's a great choice for everyday use. It comes with both hot and cold foaming options, and it's easy to clean, too. Yes, a handle would make it easier to grip, and the fill markings could be clearer, but these are minor issues in an otherwise impressive package for the price. - +Great results with dairy and plant-based milk - -A little difficult to make out max fill markings - -Foamed milk takes a good while to froth - -Lacks a handle for maximum ease when pouring Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. As my millennial colleagues often say: "you don’t wanna see me before my morning coffee". And there's truth to that: having a cappuccino on first waking has become something of a ritual for me; it's more effective than an alarm clock for getting me up and doing anything useful, at least. And since getting my hands on the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus, making a quick drink every day has never been so easy. As the name suggests, the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus is an incredibly simple to use, and it’s ideal for anyone who wants to whip up a cold or hot caffeinated beverage at home. It comes with four settings: hot milk, foamed milk, hot cappuccino, and cold cappuccino. I’ve tried all of these out over a month-long period of testing, using both dairy and plant-based milks. Should you get one for yourself? Here’s my verdict. Straight off the bat, something I love about the MilkEasy Plus are its controls. A single backlit button enables you to cycle through the four different modes. Just select your preferred option, wait a few seconds, and the frothing will begin. This makes it an accessible option for anyone — no matter their level of technical or coffee know-how. Elsewhere, the included instructions are clear and concise, and after an initial clean cycle, all you have to do is plug the machine’s dock into a power outlet, place the MilkEasy Plus on top, and you’re good to go. This model comes with a magnetic whisk that easily slots inside the MilkEasy Plus — no awkward installation required. The fact that it's magnetic means that it’s also easy to remove and clean. I was able to scrub the entire device in mere seconds, and while some pesky milk residue can stick to the sides of the MilkEasy Plus, it’s really easy to get off. The whisk and lid are also dishwasher-safe, although the main chamber needs to be hand-washed. So yes, the MilkEasy Plus is a joy to use, but how does it perform? Well, I was really happy with the results every single time. With dairy milk in cappuccino mode, it whisked up a delightfully thick, creamy foam, which delivered a rich, satisfying flavor. With foamed milk, I was impressed once more, both with dairy and plant-based milks. All those plant-based baristas will be pleased to learn that this this model is "approved by Alpro", and when using oat milk, this machine really shines. The smooth, velvety texture of the foamed milk was impressive given the modest price of this model, although it did take a good three minutes to prepare. This wasn’t a big issue for me, as I set the foaming cycle in motion before drawing an espresso shot from my Lavazza A Modo Mio Smeg machine, meaning I wasn’t left waiting. But if you want the speediest performance possible, this might not be the best option for you. Not surprisingly, the hot milk and cold cappuccino modes produced similarly effective results with dairy and plant-based milk. And I was struck by how quiet the MilkEasy Plus is in use — you won't have to worry about disturbing any friends or family members if you’re making a late-night decaf coffee. While I had an overwhelmingly positive experience with the MilkEasy Plus, I do have a couple of minor quibbles that are worth a mention. Like a lot of rivals, the markings for quantity on the inside of the cup are a little difficult to read, and I found myself having to angle the machine to see the maximum fill line when adding milk. My other critique is that the MilkEasy Plus doesn't have a handle, so it can be slightly awkward to handle while pouring. This isn’t a major problem, and it’s still easy enough to grip, but a handle would have taken things up a notch. Still, this model's build quality is impressive, especially given its relatively low £79 / AU$119 (about $100) list price. The quality of the MilkEasy Plus’ results, its user-friendly controls, and easy cleaning all combine to make it a top-tier option. And while a steam wand will always be superior for latte art, this model is tough to beat for casual coffee drinkers like me. Lavazza MilkEasy Plus review: price & release date - Priced at £79 / AU$119 (about $100) The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus was released in July 2026, and is available in the UK, a number of European markets, and Australia. It isn't available directly in the US, but could conceivably be imported. This is a relatively budget-friendly model, coming in at £79 / AU$119 (about $100), making it cheaper than some of our favorite picks such as the Smeg Mini Milk Frother (£99.95, about $140 / AU$210) and the Dreo Baristamaker ($99 / £119.99, about AU$150). Should I buy the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus? The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus has both hot and cold foaming capabilities, and produces great results across the board. Just press the backlit button, select your preferred type, and your milk will be ready in minutes. You want a simple and easy-to-clean machine The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus is very easy to clean. The transparent lid and whisk can be placed in the dishwasher, and the main chamber can be hand-washed in a matter of seconds. The dock can’t be submerged in water, though, so wipe it clean with a wet or dry cloth instead. The MilkEasy Plus produces thick, creamy results, but it perhaps lacks the close-control that a steam-wand provides for doing latte art. You want the speediest performance around While the MilkEasy Plus is a smooth, quiet operator, it’s not the speediest performer around. It took a good few minutes for a foamed milk cycle to finish. For more instant results, you may want to look elsewhere. Lavazza MilkEasy Plus review: also consider This machine shares a lot of similarities with the MilkEasy Plus. It's simple to use, produces thick hot or cold foam that would work well for regular or iced cappuccinos, and it can be cleaned in a matter of seconds. Its compact and sleek design also helps it to stand out from a lot of the competition. Read our full Smeg Mini Milk Frother review. While the Dreo Baristamaker is on the bulky side, we were really impressed by its consistent results, quiet operation, and ease of use. If you want a higher maximum milk capacity, this is a great alternative to the MilkEasy Plus. Read our full Dreo Baristamaker review. I spent one month testing the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus, using it as a key part of my coffee-making setup almost every day. I tried all four of the frothing modes, and made sure to use whole and semi-skimmed milk, as well as oat milk to assess consistency across different types. I used the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus alongside my Lavazza A Modo Mio Smeg capsule coffee machine for this review. More generally, I’ve spent years testing gadgets here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve tested everything from home products such as the Dreo Smart Misting Fan 516S to Dolby Atmos soundbars, like the Marshall Heston 120.

item.title: REVIEW: IQUNIX MQ80 low profile mechanical keyboard review
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The IQUNIX MQ80 is well-made and super stylish, but it’s not quite the instant sell it used to be. Catch this one if you don’t like magnetic switches, but otherwise wait for a sale. - +Aluminum construction and PBT keycaps make it incredibly durable - +Gasket mounted for soft keystrokes and enhanced acoustics - +Excellent sound, feel, and responsiveness - -Switches aren’t adjustable, limited options available Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. When it comes to mechanical keyboards, IQUNIX has always been ahead of the curve. Before COVID turned the mainstream onto mechanical keyboards, the company had already been releasing some of the best mechanical keyboards available, quietly making the case for PBT keycaps and premium materials that have since become the norm. With a catalog of traditional mechanical keyboards under its belt, it’s not surprising that the company would be ready to branch into new territory. It has the Hall Effect demographic covered with its EZ series, but the MQ80 goes another direction entirely. It takes all of the lessons the company learned about how to create an exceptional typing and gaming experience and compressed it. It’s all aluminum, low profile, and offers some of the best-sounding keystrokes of its kind, but steep competition and poor portability hold it back from being the go-to pick it might otherwise be. Design and Construction of the IQUNIX MQ80 The IQUNIX MQ80 breaks the mold for IQUNIX, but carries the same 75-percent layout as countless mechanical keyboards before it. The form factor is sometimes referred to as a “Compact TKL,” since it shares most of the same keys — minus the blank spaces in between. The result is a condensed slab of keys, including a full function row, arrow cluster, and seven navigation and editing keys. Nothing too out of the ordinary there, but the MQ80 marries that compact layout with an impressively low height of only 0.4 inches (10.8mm) at the front and 1.08 inches (27.5mm) in the rear. The keycaps are the same height across every row, and while they're scooped to keep your finger centered above the switch, they otherwise feel identical below the finger tip. This makes it an easy transition if you’re coming from a laptop or Apple Magic Keyboard, but first-time LP users should be prepared for a learning curve. The keyboard is wireless and supports both 2.4GHz and Bluetooth 5.1 connections, as well as wired if you need to use it while it’s recharging. It sports a 4,000 mAh battery which IQUNIX claims can sustain the keyboard for up to 350 hours. This is with the usual caveats of that being over Bluetooth with all of the lighting disabled, etc. etc. — but I was able to use it for close to two weeks between recharges, even with the lighting on. The MQ80 is a bit of a curiosity, if I’m being honest. It's thin, yes, but it’s certainly not light. It uses a heavy, CNC-milled aluminum case, just like the company’s prior models and countless others aiming for that “premium feel.” It’s a case study in how looks can be deceiving. In fact, it has been a pretty common occurrence for people to comment on how surprising its weight is. The keyboard tips the scales at 2.6 pounds, which is around what you encounter with a full-size mechanical keyboard or nicer TKL. From a low profile keyboard that everyone assumes will be airy and effortless to carry around, it flies in the face of what you might expect. So while technically, yes, it’s a portable keyboard (IQUNIX even provides a nice hardshell carrying case to tote it around in), it's not one I could see most people wanting to carry every day. Instead, this seems designed to live on your desk, providing a solid option for fans of the profile who prefer to use it for all of their typing — not just on the go. In typical IQUNIX fashion, the MQ80 is built to an enthusiast's standard. The case features intricate milling with plenty of small accents that lend it a vaguely cyberpunk impression. The keycaps feature colored legends and contrasting accents that complete its visual identity. The keyboard is available in white or black with keycaps to match, and both look fetching. The keycaps are made of thick PBT plastic. They have a light texture to add some grip to your typing experience and use dye sublimated legends that won't chip or fade over time. The switches below those keycaps are Kailh Rose Red, a lightweight linear switch with a 40g actuation force, 2.8mm of travel distance, and a 1.2mm actuation point. Despite their shortness, they offer 70% of the movement of a full-height switch. This makes them easier to transition to in how they feel to bottom out, but they still feel sensitive. This is a keyboard to use with a light touch or you'll find yourself with strings of single letters or running from cover before you mean to. The switches are hot-swappable with any Kailh Choc V2 alternative, but there just aren't many options. Gateron has run away with the variety end of the low profile switch market, but you can swap them out if you're inclined to do so. The keyboard features per-key RGB backlighting, customizable within the VIA web configurator or with shortcut keys. The keycaps aren't backlit, however, so it's not great for use in the dark if you aren't a touch typist. The internal structure of the keyboard is where things get really interesting. The MQ80 came into the world following a run of pre-built custom keyboards IQUNIX produced under its SUPER product line. It pulled direct influence from the boutique, limited run, group buy custom keyboards popular on r/mechanicalkeyboards. All of those lessons come into play with the MQ80. Beneath the keys lies a multi-layer assembly that makes even the best gaming keyboards look simple in comparison. It's an intentional system meant to filter and refine the sound and feel of every keystroke without the need to customize or adjust anything yourself. Moving from the top down, the switches snap into a fiberglass (FR4) plate, a middle-ground material that balances firmness with crisp keystrokes. Beneath the plate and PCB are two layers of foam, each with different acoustic properties, and a plastic film. The first layer of foam is thick PORON and fills in the empty space between the switches, plate, and PCB. It cuts reverb and helps isolate each switch. A much thinner, less dense sheet of IXPE foam and a plastic PET sheet sit below the switches to add a crispness and pop to each keystroke. Below the circuit board is another layer of PORON foam that filters soundwaves that pass through and cushion each press. Finally, in the very bottom of the case is another layer of IXPE foam intended to reflect mid-range sounds and act as a final buffer before hitting the aluminum of the case. It sounds like a lot and it is, but it doesn't end there. The PCB assembly attaches to the case with a modified gasket mount ("Le-Tray Gasket Mount") that imparts some of the qualities of gasket mounting into this much slimmer design. Six arms from the assembly attach to the case with silicone buffers, holding it aloft to deliver pillowy bottom outs. As a wireless keyboard, IQUNIX also had to fit a battery into its slim frame. It's surprisingly large given the space constraints with a 4,000mAh capacity. This translates into 350 hours of rated uptime, but only when using Bluetooth and no RGB backlighting. In practice, keeping RGB on high and using 2.4GHz, it lasts around 45 hours but your specific figure will depend on use. While there's an obvious pre-requisite to prefer low profile keys, you'll also need to be a fan of linear switches. And not just that, you'll need to be a fan of lightweight, fast actuating low profile switches with keycaps that feel identical under your fingers. If I sound a little salty, I'm not. It's just that I've used hundreds of mechanical keyboards and typed A Song of Ice and Fire worth of words on them, including more than a fair share of competing low profile keyboards, and it's still a pain in the ass to switch back to them. At least at first, because you do get used to it and the light touch required. Before long, I remembered to pay special attention to the navigation bumps on the "F" and "J" keys. Once everything clicked, I honestly felt faster and more nimble as a typist. Surprisingly, this didn't translate into actual WPM in my case. I average right around 110 WPM on my day-to-day full height keyboard. Swapping to the MQ80, my raw speed increased slightly, likely due to the lightweight switches and the floating posture I adopted to accommodate its height. My actual average words-per-minute on MonkeyType actually decreased to 105 WPM due to having to backspace to correct typos. So, typing speed is a bit of a wash (at least for me) but it's hard to argue that the sound and feel of typing on the keyboard is less than exceptional. The multiple layers of sound dampening quiet and deepen the sound of each keystroke in a satisfying way. The Le-Tray Gasket Mount system also gives bottom outs a softness that's reminiscent of, but slightly stiffer than, the gasket mounts used on most full height gaming keyboards. The thing is, since IQUNIX launched the MQ80 to Kickstarter in early 2025, Nuphy released the third iteration of its Air75 series, the Air75 V3, and it delivers a typing experience that I feel is at least as good and is objectively more customizable with its Gateron low profile switches and tactile and silent switch options at checkout. As a heavy handed typist, I prefer a lot of tactility, especially on a keyboard with perfectly flat rows. The only option for "not a light tactile" were Kailh Black Cloud switches and would have run me half the cost of the keyboard itself. None of this is to say that the typing experience is bad. It's genuinely not. IQUNIX knows its stuff. All of this is simply to say that there's an important trade-off and if you don't like light linear switches or paying a premium to replace them, the MQ80 probably isn't the keyboard for you. If you like that light touch, the custom keyboard-esque feel of its keystrokes filtering through all of that foam and milled aluminum, then you're probably going to love it. Most of the same considerations from the typing experience apply to gaming as well, but fragging enemies is really where the MQ80 felt most at home to me. Those lightweight switches that were a liability to typing accuracy suddenly feel like hair triggers. If you're connected using the 2.4 GHz dongle or plugged in via USB, its 1,000 Hz polling rate ensures that every keystroke comes through instantly - though, it still doesn't compare to the growing number of 8,000 Hz keyboards out there on paper. Whether you'll be able to tell the difference is up for debate. While the layers of cushioning and damping don't have a direct impact on how effective the MQ80 is for gaming, much like typing, they just make the experience that much more pleasant. Apart from its switches, there's a dearth of dedicated gaming features unique to the keyboard. The keys are reprogrammable and support string macros, but you won't find a fancy software suite to support the experience here. Instead, IQUNIX went open source and the MQ80 is better for it. Where the MQ80 comes into its own is its programmability. Unlike many traditional gaming keyboards, it doesn't have downloadable software that needs to stay running in the background. Instead, IQUNIX opted to support VIA, a web-based configurator that allows you to make changes on the fly while also saving them to the keyboard. It's simple on the surface, but is surprisingly powerful once you dive into it. Every key can carry up to four different actions or macros, broken into layers for quick shortcut access. Much like holding Shift, you hold or tap a key of your choice and access those additional layers of keymaps. While this functionality isn't unique to VIA or the MQ80 by any means, big gaming companies usually require you to keep their software running to access layered functions (ex. Razer HyperShift). Here, every change is written directly to the keyboard's firmware and will work on any machine, exactly as programmed. The web client itself is fairly simple. You have a graphic of your keyboard layout with all of your current mappings on display. Underneath are all of the different commands that can be mapped, including things like media controls, additional F-keys (all the way to F24), macros, RGB controls, and virtually anything else you might want to assign to a keystroke. The biggest feature you'll miss out on, apart from proprietary features like game-synced RGB backlighting, is the ability to assign backlight colors to individual keys. It's possible to change the brightness, hue, and saturation across its dozen or so preset animations, but creating an entirely custom lighting scheme requires creating your own code and flashing it to the keyboard manually. The IQUNIX MQ80 is a very good keyboard. For a lot of users, I'm confident that they would describe it as "Great" or even "Amazing." I wouldn't fault them for that. This is essentially the luxury option in the low profile space at this point. But it's too heavy to easily tote around without questioning your life choices. If portability is important to you, I highly recommend the Nuphy Air75 V3. Or, if you're looking for something a little more office friendly than the Nuphy, the Lofree Flow 2 is another great choice that also comes with a tactile switch option. At the end of the day, all three of these options are good for the money but only the MQ80 feels like a luxury option thanks to its heavy case. If you're not planning on carrying it back and forth to work and you like a fast switch, the MQ80 is a solid choice.

item.title: SALES: Customizable split mechanical keyboard with integrated central touchpad goes on preorder for $160 — and this 3-pound slab is wireless and doesn't come with an infamous Copilot key
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
- Vantex V1 central touchpad eliminates the need to reach for a separate mouse - Vantex offers wired and wireless packages starting at $129 and $159, respectively - The V1 has 60 keys, four programmable layers, and an aluminium body Vantex has introduced the V1, a mechanical keyboard incorporating a central touchpad that lets users control their computer without reaching for a separate mouse. The keyboard measures 30.74 × 13.74 × 3.48 cm, weighs approximately 1.57 kg, and has a rearward incline of 7°. This device packs 60 keys and four programmable layers into a CNC-machined aluminium body with a durable powder-coated finish, designed for office keyboard users. A split keyboard with integrated navigation The V1 uses a split key arrangement, leaving space between both sections for a 45 × 45 mm touch-sensitive surface for cursor movement. Users can switch between typing and pointing without moving their hands far from the keyboard. Vantex says its wired prototype has undergone testing with Windows, macOS and Linux, while connectivity options include USB-C, Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz wireless. The wireless model has a 4,000 mAh battery, but its operating duration and connection performance remain under evaluation. Its mechanical switches support replacement without soldering, while a gasket-mounted construction cushions keystrokes, offering features that may interest gaming keyboard enthusiasts. The PBT keycaps use dye sublimation printing, and their layouts can be customized using an included interchangeable keycap collection. This device comes with white linear switches that have an actuation force of 42 ± 3 gf, a bottom-out force of 47 ± 5 gf, and a stated lifespan of 50 million keystrokes Early pledges offer discounts before production The Kickstarter campaign lists an introductory price of $129 for the wired package, about 50% off the regular price of $259. That package includes the keyboard without fitted keycaps, 148 keycaps and a data cable, requiring buyers to install their preferred arrangement themselves. A two-keyboard wired bundle costs $239, against a listed retail price of $518, while the wireless package starts at $159. Buyers seeking wireless connectivity can select a two-keyboard bundle priced at $299, which is 50% off the advertised standard price of $598. The wireless version is still in development, so its real-world performance can’t be guaranteed, and backers should weigh that risk before pledging. Unlike many newer Windows keyboards, the Vantex V1 does not include Microsoft's dedicated Copilot key. This omission may appeal to users who prefer conventional keyboard controls without a dedicated button for launching Microsoft's AI assistant. According to Vantex, it is still evaluating battery capacity, runtime, and connectivity for wireless operation. The company has identified component availability, assembly consistency, final testing, packaging and international shipping as potential sources of production delays. Vantex also discloses using AI-assisted tools for promotional writing, visual design and image enhancement, suggesting that the campaign materials may not represent the actual product. At the time of writing, the Vantex V1 Kickstarter campaign has raised $2,556 from 19 backers, exceeding its $637 funding goal with 27 days remaining before it closes. Potential backers should carefully evaluate the details and proceed at their own discretion.
