item.title: SALES: The hottest AI wearables and gadgets you should know about
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
A slew of AI-powered gadgets on the market aims to integrate artificial intelligence into our daily lives like never before. Some of these AI wearables — including necklaces, rings, and wristbands, as well as portable devices — serve as productivity tools, while others claim to act as friendly companions listening to your everyday thoughts. Even OpenAI is working on a compact AI companion device. Below, we’ve rounded up some of the most notable devices. Bee is an affordable pendant priced at $49.99 that can either be clipped to your clothing or worn like a fitness band. This device records everything it hears and learns your routines and preferences to create reminders and notes for you. It even features a mute button for those times you want some privacy. The companion app (currently available only on iOS) is included with a $19 monthly subscription. The app allows you to interact with Bee directly and ask it questions. You can also get key takeaways from your day and chronological transcripts of your conversations. Amazon acquired the wearables startup in July 2025, launching its first new products earlier this month. Amazon introduced two new devices: the Bee Frontier, priced at $74.99, which can be worn on the wrist or clipped to clothing, and the Bee Eclipse, priced at $99.99, a credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of a smartphone. Both offer the same core functionality as the previous generation, positioning Bee as a more affordable alternative to AI devices such as the Plaud Note and Plaud NotePin. Users can also choose to connect Bee to Alexa. Friend is one of the most hyped entrants in the “personal AI” device market. This $129 white pendant hangs around your neck and functions as an emotional support companion. It recognizes your tone and mood, allowing you to chat with it as if it were a friend. It connects to your phone via Bluetooth and constantly listens, ready to respond or send you proactive messages, like wishing you good luck before an interview. However, it has also faced criticism, including backlash against its subway ad campaign in NYC. People vandalized the ads, writing messages like “surveillance capitalism.” Likely as an attempt to stay relevant, the company recently unveiled a major product update, introducing a new voice feature. Under the name “Friend 2.0,” the updated device includes a built-in speaker that allows it to communicate with users and express a more distinctive personality. Formerly known as Rewind, Limitless is another conversation-recording pendant priced at $99. This device continuously listens, transcribing meetings, calls, and conversations (with consent) into searchable and summarized knowledge. It’s ideal for professionals, especially journalists, looking to recall important discussions. The companion app comes with 10 hours of AI features per month — such as transcription and summaries — with the option to unlock unlimited features for $29 per month. Meta introduced its first AI wearable in September, offering a new way for users to access its personal AI assistant, Muse. The device has not yet shipped, but it is expected to feature Jolly, a playful digital avatar that represents the AI assistant. Housed in a pocket-sized device that can be carried around or attached to a keychain, the wearable includes a miniature display showing the avatar. Users will be able to interact with Muse through voice commands and have it complete tasks for them. Nirva is a startup founded by former Meta Reality Labs employees, building an AI wearable focused on personal growth rather than productivity or meeting notes. Worn as a pendant or bracelet, the device listens to the wearer’s speech and uses AI to turn everyday experiences into a personal journal, helping users better understand their emotions, communication style, and habits. Through its companion app, users can explore patterns in their behavior, gain insights into how they communicate, and find ways to improve. Nirva plans to open orders in November, with shipments to early users targeted for the end of the year. The device will cost $249. Priced at $89, this device can answer your questions, summarize your conversations, create to-do lists, and help schedule meetings. Additionally, Omi is constantly listening and running your conversations through ChatGPT, allowing it to remember the context about you and offer personalized advice. Omi can be worn as a necklace, but another notable aspect is that it can be attached to the side of your head with medical tape and can detect when you’re speaking to it. At $159, Plaud’s NotePin is one of the pricier options on this list; however, its built-in AI transcription and summarization features make it a valuable tool for lawyers, journalists, and students attending meetings or lectures. The tiny wearable voice recorder can be worn on your wrist or attached magnetically to your clothing. The recordings are saved in real time on your phone, eliminating the hassle of manual note-taking. The device includes 300 free monthly transcription minutes, but with the $8.33 per month Pro plan, you upgrade your transcription time to 1,200 minutes. This year, the company is gearing up to launch a $179 ultra-thin note-taking device called the Plaud Note Pro, which is now available for preorder. Rabbit R1 is another AI gadget that has quickly become a topic of interest in the tech world, despite facing some challenges during its initial launch. This small, retro-styled handheld device features a touchscreen and rotating camera, at a price point of $199. The device is designed to be phone-adjacent, allowing you to perform tasks such as booking flights, ordering meals, and controlling apps without needing to pull out your phone each time. Following a crucial software update that rectified previous performance issues, the Rabbit R1 now boasts expanded AI features. For instance, it introduces “Creations,” a feature that allows you to build your own tools and even games. Sandbar emerged from stealth last year, unveiling the Stream ring, an AI wearable designed for note-taking. item.title: SALES: 19 best places to visit in January 2027: for warm weather, icy mountains or buzzy city breaks
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I will die on this hill: January is the most depressing month of the year when you live in Europe or on the East Coast of the United States – which makes it the perfect time to organise a lovely trip. And the good news is, you're spoilt for choice when it comes to the best places to visit in January. All the fun and good food of the Christmas festivities are now a distant memory, summer is still incredibly far away, and if we add the terrible weather and everyone trying to ‘be healthy’ after the excesses of December, the only way to get some joy in January is to hop on a plane – whether that’s a long-haul flight to a sunny Caribbean island or a short flight to the Alps to enjoy both the skiing and the après-ski. Personally, I like a bit of both. During particularly harsh winters, I always long to be in Latin America, having breakfast with plenty of pão de queijo and a fresh açaí bowl in Brazil, or eating tacos and drinking micheladas in Mexico. When autumn has been particularly mild, as it has this year, I'm partial to a week of skiing – mainly hitting the spa and happily participating in raclette parties, if I'm being honest – in the French Alps. The possibilities are endless and, interestingly, January is actually one of the best months to explore some of the world's most beautiful destinations, whether you're after winter sunshine or snow-covered mountains. In Southeast Asia and across the Caribbean, sunny skies, warm temperatures and idyllic beaches make for the perfect escape from the European winter. Closer to home, lean into the winter weather in Europe's snow-clad landscapes, whizzing on skis across the Dolomites or chasing the northern lights in Iceland. To really start the year off right, consider jetting off to one of these destinations in the last few days of December, just in time to see world-famous firework displays on New Year's Eve in Dubai, for example. Without further ado, here are the best holiday destinations to head to in January 2027.

item.title: SALES: Where to Stay When Visiting Alaska's Denali National Park
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
With broad river valleys, colorful meadows peppered with fireweed and lupine, forests thick with spruce and aspen, and the snow-covered Alaska Range rising in the distance, Denali National Park and Preserve is one of those places that can still feel startlingly wild no matter how many times you visit. At 6.1 million acres, it’s larger than Massachusetts, and the sheer scale of the national park means a trip here can look very different depending on where you choose to stay. I lived in Alaska full-time for eight years (and now split my time between Alaska and Colorado) and have been to Denali often. Over time, I got to know the best places travelers can base themselves in and around the park. The challenge of planning a trip to Denali isn’t necessarily finding somewhere to stay, but figuring out which part of the vast region makes the most sense as a home base for what you want to see. The cluster of lodges just outside the entrance, where restaurants, outfitters, and bus departures are all close at hand, is one of the go-to spots for first-time visitors. Nearby Healy and the long stretches of the Parks Highway offer more breathing room, with cabins, vacation rentals, and quieter stays scattered north and south of the park. And for travelers who want to go much deeper, Kantishna sits nearly 90 miles down Denali Park Road, offering a handful of remote lodges and the rare chance to stay deep inside the national park itself. I’ve selected the best stays across that spectrum, from full-service hotels and family-friendly cabins to secluded backcountry lodges and even a chalet set on a glacier just miles from the summit of North America’s highest peak. Read on for my favorite places to stay near Denali National Park in Alaska. How to plan a trip to Denali National Park and Preserve How do you get to Denali National Park? There is just one major highway leading to Denali National Park: George Parks Highway, which connects Denali to Fairbanks, about two and a half hours to the north, and Anchorage, about four and a half hours to the south. Both cities have well-connected airports and multiple car rental options. You don't need a car to get around in Denali National Park, but if you visit during the shoulder season, you can drive your own vehicle as far into the park as road conditions allow. If you don't want to drive, limited motor coach services can get you to Denali during the summer. The most luxurious option for reaching Denali is the Alaska Railroad, which, like the George Parks Highway, runs from Anchorage to Fairbanks and vice versa. The train runs directly through Denali's entrance and drops visitors off just a five-minute walk from the park's visitor center. When is the best time to visit Denali National Park? Denali National Park's peak season is mid-May through mid-September. Most tour, lodging, and restaurant amenities shut down as soon as the peak season ends, but if you're prepared to DIY a trip in winter conditions—or want to book a day tour out of Fairbanks—you can still visit during the winter. Visiting during the early-May or mid- to late-September shoulder seasons offers a more secluded experience. Amenities and tour options are extremely limited, but September in particular is a beautiful time for exploring the park when the weather cooperates. What are the best things to do in Denali National Park? Perhaps the best-known excursion in Denali is taking a bus ride on the lone road running into the park. Narrated tour buses and hop-on, hop-off transit buses used to run all the way down the 92-mile park road—but an ongoing land slump has forced partial closure of the road, so all vehicle traffic currently turns around at mile 43. For a quick (and free) taste of the park road, you can catch the courtesy shuttle that runs between the Denali Visitor Center and Savage River (mile 15 of the park road). You can also rent a bicycle from Bike Denali, about a (bikeable) mile outside the park entrance, and explore as far as you'd like along the park road, or drive your personal vehicle as far as mile 15 during peak season, although the small parking area at Savage River fills up fast. It's natural to expect a glimpse of North America's tallest mountain, Denali, when you come to the park that bears its name. But you'll have to venture to at least mile 9 of the park road before the elevation is high enough to reveal 20,310' Denali. If you're feeling adventurous, you can also hike to the top of the aptly named Mountain Vista trail, at about mile 12, for more views. The mountain is often obscured by clouds, so if you don't get to see it while in the park, don't despair: You can also catch a glimpse from the Alaska Railroad trains or, if you're driving, from several well-marked waysides along the Parks Highway. Denali is home to a handful of beautiful hiking trails, including the beloved Savage River and Savage Alpine trails, as well as the stunning Triple Lakes Trail, where you might be able to add beavers to your wildlife-viewing checklist. You're also welcome to hike off-trail from the park road—just hop off at any likely-looking pullout and explore. No matter where you hike, it's important that you carry bear spray—which you can rent from the Alaska Geographic store in the park, next to the Denali Visitor Center—and know what to do if you encounter wildlife. Park rangers are also available to help you choose a hiking destination and coach you on how to handle wildlife encounters. They also lead a variety of group activities, including hikes both on- and off-trail. Denali National Park is home to the National Park Service's only working kennel of sled dogs. Rangers demonstrate how they work with the dogs two to three times per day throughout the summer; you can walk to the kennels from the park entrance, or catch a free shuttle bus. You'll see a wide variety of other tour options advertised for Denali National Park, including whitewater rafting, horseback riding, ATV tours, and jeep tours. With very few exceptions, these take place along the boundary of the park, not actually in it. But adventuring alongside Denali can be a fine—and thrilling—way to spend your visit. Among companies operating just outside the park, Denali Horseback Tours is a perennial favorite. Their reliable steeds take you off into the hills for beautiful vistas overlooking the park and neighboring lands, without any of the noise or exhaust from a jeep or ATV tour. If you do want the thrill of a motor-driven vehicle, though, Denali ATV Adventures is hugely popular. A last (and favorite) way of seeing Denali at near-distance is from the water. Whitewater rafting tours from companies like the family-owned Denali Raft Adventures take you down the Nenana River, which forms the natural boundary on the east side of Denali National Park. Rafting excursions range from pulse-pounding to relatively sedate, so there’s something for almost everybody. If you’re ready to splurge on a once-in-a-lifetime experience, Alaska Alpine Adventures is an excellent guide service that does have the required permits to work inside the park. Just note that their custom hiking and backpacking tours demand a fairly high level of physical fitness. What area should you stay in near Denali National Park? Denali National Park is notably absent of a traditional gateway town, a characteristic that sets it apart from many other national parks. The National Park Service's focus on preserving the park's natural state has led to policies that limit large-scale development and urbanization. The best areas to stay in therefore include spots directly on the mountain; in Kantishna, a bustling gold mining hub situated 90 miles into the park; and a smattering of hotels, resorts, and Airbnbs between Healy (about 11 miles north of the park entrance) and Cantwell (approximately 30 miles south of the park entrance). You can also choose to stay in Talkeetna, about a two-and-a-half-hour drive from the entrance, roughly halfway between Anchorage and Denali. Keep in mind that if you plan to head to Kantishna, with the closure of the Denali Park Road beyond mile 43 until at least summer 2027 due to the Pretty Rocks Landslide, the only way to get there is currently by bush plane or helicopter, providing guests with rare, near-exclusive access to the park’s wild interior. “The Canyon” (otherwise known as “Glitter Gulch,” the hub for tourism just outside the park, with various services, tour companies, shops, and restaurants catering to visitors), is an area that exists almost exclusively for tourism—locals don’t live there. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Lisa Maloney.

item.title: SALES: I’ve Lived In The Alps For Six Seasons. These Are The European Resorts Actually Worth Your Time—and Money.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
More Americans are traveling to the Alps than ever before. At the same time, the conditions surrounding travel plans are changing rapidly. Snow coverage is dwindling, the dollar is losing value, and more U.S. based megapasses are Americans are using their megapasses overseas. Having spent several winters (and summers) in the Alps, I’m in a good place to consider everything the prospective American tourist needs to know when planning a trip. With a super El Niño forecasted for the coming season, snow coverage at Alps resorts is likely to be more relevant this year than ever before. Like the Western U.S., seasonal models are forecasting a warm and wet winter for the continent. I’ll take that over a warm and dry winter, but it’s not ideal. Once upon a time, slopes above 1,650 feet were plastered in snow on a regular basis, especially on the northern side of the Alps. Unfortunately, those days are over. That means some lower destinations are far less attractive than they used to be, especially for Americans who usually have to lock in flights and accommodation months in advance. Take Portes du Soleil. With 360 miles of pistes and essentially unlimited off-piste straddling both France and Switzerland, the ski area is one of the world’s largest ski domains. Despite the size, the resort peaks at just 7,200 feet. With base elevations of around 3,300 feet, many storms now bring rain to the lower slopes instead of snow. These days, it’s not uncommon to have rain above 6,500 feet anywhere in the French Alps. Austria is somewhat more continental and protected when warm air surges from the south and west. However, many of its most famous ski resorts sit at relatively low altitudes, and skiing has taken a hit in recent years. Kitzbühel, a big name in ski racing and one of the most famous Austrian resorts for Americans, is ideal in many ways. It embodies European skiing, with a beautiful base village, endless terrain, great après-ski, and a formidable ski history. It’s also on the Ikon Pass. But the resort tops out at just 6,600 feet, with a base elevation of 2,625 feet. Saalbach Skicircus is another legendary Austrian resort, with 168 miles of piste and some of the country’s best off-piste skiing. Epic Pass holders get 5 days here. Nevertheless, with similar elevations to Kitzbühel, the good days, especially off-piste, are more limited than ever. If the weather lines up with a nordstau (European equivalent to Northwest flow bringing in heavy snow) and low snow coverage in Austria, and travel plans are flexible, Americans will love these resorts. But I wouldn’t gamble on booking an overseas trip too far in advance. This is the year to focus on resorts that top out above 10,000 feet in France, Italy, and Switzerland, and above 8,200 feet in Austria. Nearly every American I meet in the Alps has one of two destinations on their itinerary: Chamonix or Zermatt. These towns are burned into the American mountain consciousness, and they’re both on the Ikon Pass, though Chamonix comes with some fine print. But are they worth it? Chamonix is the birthplace of mountaineering. To some extent, it’s also the birthplace of the winter sports industry. The first Winter Olympics were held there in 1924. Chamonix is credited with heralding a new age for dying mountain towns, with a “white gold” rush of winter sports infrastructure throughout the Alps and beyond. There’s clearly history here, but I don’t think that Chamonix is the ideal destination for most Americans looking to head to the Alps for a skiing-focused trip. For starters, the Ikon Pass only includes the Chamonix “Le Pass,” not the Mont-Blanc Unlimited. That’s some annoying fine print that means you can’t ski at the Aiguille du Midi (so no famous Vallée Blanche), Courmayeur (Skyway Monte Bianco), or the top station of the Grands Montets (burned down in 2018 but returning in 2027-’28). Those are the three best things to do when you go to Chamonix. The Unlimited pass is around $80 USD, but like most resorts, prices fluctuate. Instead, “Le Pass” comes with standard access to the five resorts of the Chamonix Valley, which are decent, but not outstanding within the context of the Alps. With Le Pass, the highest access is only 9,186 feet off the Bouchard gondola at the Grands Montets. Getting around between the resorts is punishing during high season. To do the Vallée Blanche or Skyway, you’ll have to splurge an additional 90 Euros ($103 at press time) for a Mont Blanc Unlimited. Meanwhile, Zermatt has long been a stronghold of U.S. tourists. Americans originally discovered Switzerland during vacations after WWII. Today, Zermatt is still full of Americans. For one, it’s on the Ikon Pass. It’s also expensive, but American skiers know how to handle high prices better than most. For some people, waking up with views of the Matterhorn is a bucket list experience. Zermatt is a world-class ski resort with broad, snowsure pistes, fast lifts, and insane views. For the money, however, you can get a less iconic but more quintessential experience in plenty of other places. Though the biggest issue for Zermatt is cost—it feels at least twice as expensive as France—other aspects fall short as well. The food is mediocre compared to France and Italy. The skiing is exposed, cold, and limited on stormy days. Despite being snowsure due to its altitude, Zermatt is not the snowiest place in the Alps. Off-piste is more easily accessible at other resorts. Each Alpine country offers its own blend of culture, pricing, efficiency, access, and more. You’ll have to weigh which factors will make the best vacation for you. France and Italy offer the best food and prices, but you’ll find that things don’t always run as efficiently. Lifts and restaurants may be randomly closed (fermature exceptionelle!), and service isn’t always up to the standard you’d expect in America. In comparison, Switzerland and Austria operate much more efficiently and, generally speaking, receive more snow than France and Italy. Historically, the northern Alps receive the most snow, with resorts like Engelberg and St. Anton tallying the highest numbers. However, signs suggest this climate regime may be changing, and recent years have seen more storms coming from the south. Switzerland and Austria also have the best lifts—most of the existing and planned 3S cable cars in the Alps are here. (The only 3S cable car in North America is Whistler’s Peak2Peak.) In France, and maybe in the world, Tignes/Val d’Isère is the best ski resort for the most people. The skiing offers something for everyone, from toddlers learning to ski to extreme freeriders. The Grand Motte chair accesses glacier terrain at 11,339 feet, the fifth-highest cable car in the Alps. Val d’Isère is a traditional village (culture!), not just a purpose-built ski resort, and the new development is limited to Tignes. Moreover, the base of 5,906 feet is one of the highest for a big resort in the Alps. With about three million American skiers on the Epic and Ikon passes, the only downside is that Tignes/Val d’Isère isn’t included on either—or perhaps that’s a plus, if you’re looking to avoid other Americans. It’s expensive by French standards, but far cheaper than anything you’ll find in Switzerland. Day tickets hover around $80 for adults. Meanwhile, Americans have shifted toward Trois Vallées in recent years. Trois Vallées is one of the best resorts on the Epic Pass—it’s one of the world’s largest, with endless pistes and backcountry terrain alike. Paradiski, consisting of Les Arcs and La Plagne, is another large resort between Trois Vallées and Val d’Isère. Overshadowed by its more famous neighbors, it’s still a fantastic, massive domain with slightly more competitive prices ($66-$85 for adults per day). Most Americans never make it farther south than the Savoie. But that’s precisely where the French Alps begin—at least in a cultural sense. Alpe d’Huez and Les 2 Alpes follow in the tradition of French megaresorts, with mediocre piste offerings but excellent off-piste. However, Serre Chevalier, near the town of Briançon, is the largest and best French resort that most Americans have never heard of. Despite its size, parts of Serre Chevalier still have a village vibe, like Monetier-les-Bains. This hamlet is home to incredible off-piste (the Montagnole) as well as fantastic pistes. The on- and off-mountain dining is also exceptional. Single-day lift tickets are around $78 for adults. Further east, on the border with Italy, is Montgenèvre ($58-$66 for an adult lift ticket). This little gem is located on a pass in the middle of the Alps, and receives snow from both the east and west. It’s also connected with the Via Lattea (see below). Going south, you’ve escaped the land of garish megaresorts and entered into parts unknown—at least for Americans. Abriès and Saint-Véran (both offer lift tickets starting around $48) are two surprisingly high (8,202 feet and 9,186 feet, respectively) resorts in the Queyras, a little-known pocket of the Alps that retains its charm. Hotel La Lobio, not far from Saint-Véran, epitomizes French country lodging and cuisine, run by a single, passionate family. A few valleys further south, Risoul, Vars, Crevoux, and Les Orres are all worthy destinations if the Alps are seeing storms from the southwest. If you’re on the hunt for the best culture—ancient villages and incredible food—and prices in the Alps, Italy should be on your list. The Epic and Ikon passes cover many of the country’s best options. The addition of Aosta Valley to the Ikon Pass means many Americans can now visit magnificent resorts like Monte Rosa, Cervinia, La Thuile, and Courmayeur. Monte Rosa (starting around $80 for a day) is a personal favorite with unlimited off-piste and ski touring from the resort. Consider lodging at some of the smaller base villages, like Alagna (best access) or Gressoney, in the upper Lys Valley. Gressoney-St.-Jean and Gressoney-La-Trinité are home to one of Italy’s few remaining Walser German–speaking populations. Cervino is an alternative to Zermatt. It’s the Italian side of Matterhorn Ski Paradise, which means you can also ski Zermatt. Currently, the crossing is a bit of a bottleneck, with limited-capacity trams serving the Plateau Rosa from the Italian side. However, the 3S cable car, called Cervino The One, is currently under construction and expected to finish by 2030, and will actually make the Klein Matterhorn faster to reach from Cervino than from Zermatt. When you combine that with much better food and prices on the Italian side, Cervino has a lot going for it. South of Aosta, you’ll find the Via Lattea ($80), a collection of several interconnected resorts, the most famous being Sestrière. It’s one of the world’s most vast ski areas, on par with Portes du Soleil and Trois Vallées. It’s not on the megapasses, and I doubt you’ll run into another American. Unfortunately, like Portes du Soleil, altitude is somewhat lacking, though Sestrière reaches 9,186 feet, and these mountains benefit from both easterly and westerly winds. The region’s standout feature is its world-class tree skiing—among the best in the Alps—if conditions allow. The dining is out of this world, even on the mountain. La Marmotta, located on the upper slopes of the Sauze d’Oulx sector, is the best food I’ve ever had on the slopes (38 Euros for a three-course meal and wine, and that’s expensive for Italy). And I’ve eaten at a lot of restaurants in the Alps. Try staying at Agriturismo Barba Gust for the most authentic Alpine ski experience you can get. The Dolomites have had the spotlight over the past year thanks to the Cortina Olympics. The Dolomiti Superski ($98), on Ikon, is still a great option for Americans—perhaps the best option in the country. These resorts don’t get the most snow, but the natural scenery of the Dolomites sets them apart from other resorts in the Alps. Because this is a collection of relatively small ski resorts, you’ll find many authentic villages rather than manufactured ski bases. Cortina is the most famous (and luxurious), but Val Gardena, Kronplatz, and Alta Badia are better for pure skiing. Like many resorts in Italy, the on-mountain dining is unreal—Baita Ciadinat, on the upper slopes of Val Gardena, is a must. Austria is a country whose national identity revolves around skiing. In fact, no country in the world has better slopes and access. The Austrian Alps are full of large, efficient ski resorts that combine high annual snowfall and medium prices—maybe just a bit more expensive than France but much less than Switzerland (and the U.S.). Austria is well-represented on the Epic and Ikon passes. While the days of unlimited fresh tracks are long gone at any resort, Austrian ski culture still tends a bit more toward the pistes. Therefore, you can often find that fresh tracks last longer here, especially on snowy days—Austrians don’t seem to like storm skiing. Austria is also holding down the après fort at a time when interest in après seems to be diminishing in the rest of the Alps. If you like loud, commercial dance music and general debauchery after a day of skiing, you’re going to want to focus your vacation search on Austria. The Epic Pass offers more in Austria than the Ikon Pass. However, Epic Pass holders receive five consecutive days at Skicircus Saalbach, Sölden, Zillertal, and Silveretta Montafon, all world-class resorts. So you could do nearly a month in Austria with the Epic, with access to close to 1,000 kms (620 miles) of pistes, several glaciers, and endless off-piste and ski touring. In my opinion, . It’s on the edge of the Alps’ most consistent snowbelt and has extensive off-piste terrain. The place is enormous, whether you want to ski on- or off-piste. Unfortunately for Americans, the Epic Pass has some fine print (you only get three consecutive days, and you have to stay at one of a few participating hotels to redeem them). In my opinion, Ski Arlberg (St. Anton) is still the gold standard of Austrian skiing. It’s on the edge of the Alps’ most consistent snowbelt and has extensive off-piste terrain. The Ikon Pass is a bit less fruitful. Ischgl ($80-$95) is a fantastic all-around resort, if a bit devoid of character. It’s also connected to Samnaun in Switzerland. Kitzbühel ($80-$93) is Austria’s signature resort, though as I mentioned earlier, its appeal as an international destination is getting hampered by its lack of altitude (same with Saalbach). I always recommend Americans check out Innsbruck. It’s a real city, offering the same benefits as the great capitals of Europe, like palaces and universities. Over 100,000 locals live here, not just an endless stream of tourists. The local resort of Nordkette is nothing to write home about, but you can easily access a dozen or so resorts on the Innsbruck Pass ($185 for a two-day pass), from low elevation all the way up to the Stubai Glacier. The city also has excellent shuttle and rail transport so that you can get anywhere in an hour. St. Anton? An hour west by train. Kitzbühel and Saalbach? An hour east by train. Austria has over 400 ski resorts, so there are plenty of secret gems to discover. Just keep an eye on the weather. Often, a ridge can set up over western Europe and keep most of the Alps dry. However, sometimes moisture can flow from the north along the backside of this ridge and make a direct hit on the eastern Austrian Alps, east of Salzburg. Resorts like Zauchensee ($86) and Obertauern ($82) are great options, and you’ll see far fewer tourists (and probably zero Americans). One of Switzerland’s biggest successes is the abundance of carless base villages. Zermatt is famous for its Gornergrat railway, but there are dozens of car-free villages, including Wengen, Saas-Fee, and Mürren. For me, though it may seem like a small detail, the absence of cars goes a long way toward making you feel as if you’d gone back in time. And that’s more valuable than ever these days. Switzerland is also the most snowsure region of the Alps, with plenty of high-altitude, north-facing slopes along the range’s north side. There’s a reason the largest glaciers in the Alps are here. The ski resorts are cozier and more specialized, which can be a pro or a con, depending on what you’re looking for. There are a few exceptions to the cozyness. Verbier ($100), one of the most well-known resorts to Americans, sprawls across four valleys and offers up some of the Alps’ most “big mountain” terrain. However, if you’re looking to ski off-piste, Verbier is home to all the most ambitious freeriders in Europe, who will snag your line before you even know it exists. By the time you figure out the lay of the land, these young guns will already be at work cooking your lunch. You’re better off going to Austria. In place of Zermatt, Americans should consider Saas Fee ($102). Like Zermatt, it’s a car-free village, but it’s much more authentic. Most chalets are hundreds of years old. The top funicular reaches 11,482 feet, though the variety of pistes does not match Zermatt. However, Saas Fee truly embodies the Swiss Valais, the canton home to Zermatt, Verbier, and other famous resorts. Andermatt ($100-$120) and Engelberg ($80-$90) are both top off-piste destinations. Unfortunately, they both only have one lift that accesses the summit, which means skier capacity is low, lift lines are long, and the limited terrain gets claimed in the blink of an eye. Laax ($47-$150) and Arosa Lenzerheide ($108) are larger resorts that are less known for their freeride offerings; however, they have more efficient lifts and fewer hungry freeriders to compete with. If you can afford it, Davos ($97-$113) and St. Moritz ($67) are also quite good for off-piste skiing, despite their reputation as luxury resorts (St. Moritz is on the Ikon Pass). Switzerland has just 23 million skier visits a year, despite having over 300 ski resorts. That’s about 100 more resorts than France, which clocks in at 51 million visits. The result is, outside of Verbier and Zermatt, a less crowded experience. Just know that it will cost you double compared to the other Alpine countries.

item.title: SALES: Six of the Greatest Movie Soundtracks From This Century
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. A great movie soundtrack can be just as memorable as the film itself. A few notes might bring an entire scene rushing back, and an old song can find new life in the right movie. Below, six Atlantic staffers share their favorite film soundtracks of the 21st century. One Battle After Another (streaming on HBO Max and Prime Video) Beneath its cat-and-mouse tale about fascism and rebellion, Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2025 Best Picture Oscar winner is a masterpiece of cadence. The story progresses in slow creeps and sudden, skittering leaps. Characters crash together and pull apart like excited molecules. The sizzling energy owes to an unusual process: Anderson hired the Radiohead multi-instrumentalist Jonny Greenwood to compose music before shooting began and then edited Greenwood’s work. The soundtrack pairs percussive piano with drums hooked to robotic circuits to create backbeats as insistent and unsteady as hiccups. Twanging guitars and symphonic strings express unsettled, ugly-pretty chords. The effect is an astonishingly original reminder that social movements are but collections of individuals, each squiggling along their own trajectory. Darkest Hour (streaming on Apple TV and Prime Video) I love soundtracks, but my favorites—Glory, Miller’s Crossing, Crimson Tide—are all at least 30 years old. I am a sucker for a John Williams march or an elegiac Thomas Newman moment, but when I consulted my playlist, I found that one soundtrack kept rising to the top: Darkest Hour, by Dario Marianelli (with piano by Víkingur Ólafsson). The movie follows Winston Churchill’s first days in office, in 1940, after France fell and Britain stood alone against the Nazis. The score alternates between piano meditations and orchestral flight; like Churchill, it is fussy and elegant, quiet and then bombastic. It conveys the tension and urgency in the man and the moment. The final track, “We Shall Fight,” plays over Churchill’s speech to Parliament in which he vows to never surrender to evil. It is a moving and uplifting piece, but also tragic: He knew the horrors that awaited, and he led Britain to its fate anyway. The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (streaming on HBO Max) On the subject of movie music, much comes to mind. My single favorite piece of original movie music this century might be “The Alien,” Ben Salisbury and Geoff Barrow’s eerie composition for Annihilation; my favorite repurposed song might be Plumtree’s “Scott Pilgrim,” the lovey-dovey indie-rock namesake of Scott Pilgrim vs. the World. Jon Brion’s off-kilter bricolage for Punch-Drunk Love, the torch ballads of A Star Is Born, the uncut Daft Punk–ness of Tron: Legacy—all of this matters to me. However, play two seconds of “Concerning Hobbits,” and I’m back in the Shire, awaiting the appearance of a great wizard and hanging out with my vertically challenged friends. Howard Shore’s score for Fellowship, and for the rest of the Lord of the Rings series, is both transportive and formfitting, making Peter Jackson’s movie sound as epic as it looks. Shrek 2 (streaming on Peacock) When I first watched Shrek 2, I was far more interested in the movie’s ridiculous fairy-tale antics than in the music. Years later, I’ve come to appreciate that the soundtrack is every bit as good as the movie itself. The song choices, including Counting Crows’ “Accidentally in Love” in the opening sequence, are absurdly perfect for a film about a green ogre meeting his in-laws. The soundtrack also features David Bowie, Nick Cave, and Tom Waits, but the undisputed highlight is Jennifer Saunders’s rendition of “Holding Out for a Hero” as the Fairy Godmother, which turns the climactic rescue scene into a musical spectacle that has no right to be as thrilling as it is. A villain belting out a Bonnie Tyler song while a giant gingerbread man storms a castle? As a kid, I thought it was the height of cinema. I may have outgrown some of my other childhood favorites, but I still think the Fairy Godmother deserves a Grammy. Challengers (streaming on Paramount+ and Apple TV) Ever need to outrun a serial killer, punch a bully, or fight a bear? Have I got the soundtrack for you! Nothing gets me going quite like Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’s magnus opus, the soundtrack for Luca Guadagnino’s film Challengers. (To fans of their work for The Social Network—sorry, this one’s simply better!) The film makes the compelling argument that everything in life is about sex, except sex, which is about tennis. The pulsing, almost panic-inducing score draws on Berlin techno and ’90s rave music to heighten the anxiety of the film’s central love triangle. The frenzied sounds amplify the adrenaline that elite tennis players feel as they play (and sometimes kiss) each other. Listening to the climactic track, “Match Point,” one almost feels like the tennis ball being flung around the court. Whenever I need to crush a deadline or motivate myself to tackle a hard task, the Challengers soundtrack is my go-to. Plus, I once heard it played in a nightclub, and I haven’t been the same since. Sicario (streaming on HBO Max and Hulu) The Icelandic composer Jóhann Jóhannsson’s work in Sicario has been ripped off a million times. The beautifully foreboding noises he pioneered and perfected for Denis Villeneuve’s ultra-stylish, very violent feds-versus-cartels thriller—the subterranean bass groans, the trapped-in-the-birth-canal percussion, the tinnitus-like swarms of strings—are now part of the standard kit of horror-movie soundtracking: You can hear them, in degraded form, everywhere. But Jóhannsson, unlike his imitators, had other registers, other capacities: Sicario also features the elegiac “Desert Music,” which sounds less like the industrial metal nihilists Godflesh and more like, I don’t know, Bach. Something else Jóhannsson shared with Bach? I think he was probably a genius.
